messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For nearly two days after he was taken, Minh remembered very little in a way that felt settled. He had immigrated to the United States from Vietnam as a child and, at 35, was working as an accountant in a midsize office where predictability had once been a relief to him. The trauma had occurred on a visit abroad to see extended family, when he was detained by men he did not know, held in a small room, and repeatedly threatened and assaulted while being questioned. What remained with him most vividly was not a coherent account but a series of sharply lit fragments: the scrape of a chair, a voice asking the same thing again, the sensation of waiting for the door to open. Even when he tried to describe what happened, the order would slip. He would begin with being grabbed on the street, jump to the room, then stop and say that maybe that was not how it had happened. At times the memory ran through his mind like a film he had not chosen to turn on, yet at the same time it felt strangely detached, as if he were watching something that had happened to another man and not to himself.

In the months after he returned home, Minh found that certain ordinary moments struck him with disproportionate force. At work, a new client walking into the office and introducing himself could leave Minh instantly guarded; he would notice the man’s tone, hands, posture, and feel a conviction settle over him that strangers were fundamentally dangerous, that there was no way to know who might harm him. He had once been polite and contained in his job, able to meet unfamiliar people without much thought, but now even brief conversation in the reception area could leave him cold and preoccupied for hours. Something similar happened whenever coworkers spoke casually about long-term plans—retirement contributions, next quarter, trips later in the year. Talk about the future did not simply make him uncomfortable. It seemed to expose how impossible the future felt to trust, and he would come away thinking not just that danger was possible, but that safety itself had been an illusion all along.

Those moments also deepened what he had come to believe about himself. Minh was increasingly certain that the ordeal had altered him in a lasting way, that whatever steadiness he once had was gone for good. He compared himself harshly to an imagined stronger person and thought somebody else would have stopped it, resisted better, found a way out before things escalated. He knew, when pressed, that he had been overpowered and isolated, but the self-criticism persisted with a punishing certainty. In his mind, the fact that he had survived did not protect him from the conclusion that he had failed some test of character. When he was caught off guard by a stranger or heard colleagues talking easily about years ahead, those beliefs intensified: the world was unsafe, he was diminished, and other people would have coped where he had not.

The more fixed these convictions became, the more disjointed his remembering seemed. When he sat alone after work trying to piece together what had happened, the memory would begin to play again in the same visual sequence, vivid and repetitive, but he could not make it into a narrative that felt like his own life. He would say that he knew intellectually the scenes were his, yet emotionally they seemed to belong to someone damaged beyond recognition. His belief that he had permanently changed for the worse appeared to sharpen that estrangement; if he was no longer the same man, then the man in the memory felt foreign too. And because he was so preoccupied with how he should have acted differently, he kept returning to isolated instants—what he said, whether he hesitated, whether there had been some moment to stop it—rather than a continuous timeline, leaving the sequence more confused each time he revisited it.

This had begun to shape his daily life in concrete ways. In the accounting office, where much of the work depended on client contact and planning ahead, Minh had started delegating introductory meetings whenever he could and keeping conversations narrowly transactional. He avoided lingering in the lobby if unfamiliar people were there. During team discussions about future projects, he sometimes went silent or excused himself under the pretense of needing to check numbers. His divorce had preceded the trauma, but he now saw it as further evidence that he was the kind of person things happened to and the kind of person who could not hold life together. He lived alone and kept his routines spare.

By the time he sought help, what frightened Minh most was not only the memory itself but the possibility that this estranged, repetitive, out-of-order version of it was all that would ever remain—that he would keep feeling ambushed by strangers, shut down by any mention of the future, and confirmed again and again in his sense that the world was unknowable and he was permanently reduced by what had been done to him. He said he wanted treatment because he was tired of feeling as if his life had already ended while he was still expected to plan for it, and because some part of him still hoped the memory could become something he remembered rather than something that kept happening.
